name: Custom bleaching trays
lead: Custom bleaching trays are thin, fitted mouthpieces made from a mould of a person's teeth, loaded with a carbamide or hydrogen peroxide gel and worn for a set period at home, usually under dentist supervision. They are used to make teeth look whiter and more even in shade, which is among the quickest ways to brighten a smile. Wikipedia credits an orthodontist with introducing tray bleaching in the late 1960s, and notes that a 1989 paper by Haywood and Heymann supported the method.[1]

Tray gels commonly use carbamide peroxide, which Wikipedia says was favoured because its effects were reported to last longer than hydrogen peroxide. Tray-based treatment is described as producing one or two shades of lightening within about three days, with worn times ranging from overnight to a few hours daily.[1]

A 2018 Cochrane review of 71 randomized trials of home-based bleaching, including tray-delivered carbamide and hydrogen peroxide gels, reported that products whitened teeth more than placebo over two weeks to six months, though the certainty of evidence was low to very low, and that sensitivity and oral irritation were the most common side effects.[3]

paras: A dentist takes an impression of the teeth and has a tray made that fits closely around them. A peroxide gel is placed in the tray, which keeps the gel against the teeth and away from much of the gum tissue.[1] Wikipedia notes that custom trays reduce the risk of gum burns that can come from ill-fitting delivery, and that bleaching gels at 10 percent hydrogen peroxide or more can injure tissue.[1] Some trays include small reservoirs on the tooth surfaces to hold extra gel.[2]

A 2018 Cochrane systematic review included 71 randomized controlled trials in adults: 26 compared a bleaching product with placebo and 51 compared one product with another. Tray-based carbamide and hydrogen peroxide gels were among the products studied, alongside strips, paint-on gels, gums and mouthwash. Compared with placebo, products whitened teeth over short periods (two weeks to six months), with low to very low certainty; head-to-head comparisons were too varied and small to show whether any product, concentration or duration was superior.[3]

The review found tooth sensitivity and oral irritation were the most common side effects, more frequent with higher concentrations but generally mild and temporary, and whitening did not change oral health-related quality of life.[3]

A laboratory study of 96 extracted molars used 10 percent and 22 percent carbamide peroxide, with and without gel reservoirs in the trays, to see whether bleaching changed the shade of pit and fissure stains on the biting surfaces.[2]

Tooth sensitivity is the most common side effect of peroxide bleaching, with Wikipedia reporting that home bleaching causes less than in-office treatment. Over-bleaching, enamel roughening and colour change of existing restorations are also described.[1]

In the EU, whitening products with more than 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide may only be applied under dental supervision (up to 6 percent), to patients 18 or over. The US FDA is described as endorsing gels below 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide.[1]

timeline.event: Custom tray bleaching introduced by an orthodontist.[1]
Haywood and Heymann publish support for tray bleaching with carbamide peroxide.[1]
Cochrane review of 71 randomized trials of home-based whitening published.[3]

card.summary: Dentist-fitted trays that hold carbamide peroxide gel against the teeth; the long-standing at-home alternative to strips.
card.aka: Take-home bleaching trays, dentist-supervised home bleaching
card.note: Sensitivity is common; poorly fitting trays are linked to gum irritation.

quick.overview:
Custom bleaching trays are mouthpieces moulded to a person's teeth and filled with a peroxide gel, typically carbamide peroxide. They have been used since the late 1960s and are usually prescribed by a dentist.

Wikipedia describes tray bleaching as producing about one or two shades of lightening within days, with some fading afterwards.
quick.mechanism: The tray keeps the oxidising gel in contact with the teeth, where the peroxide breaks down pigment molecules in enamel and dentine.
quick.risks: Sensitivity is the most common side effect; gum irritation or burns are linked to high peroxide concentrations and ill-fitting trays. EU rules allow up to 6 percent hydrogen peroxide only under dental supervision.

chain: Fitted tray holds peroxide gel against the teeth
Peroxide breaks down pigment molecules in enamel and dentine
Teeth look one to two shades lighter, with some fading over time
angle.text: The tray keeps gel in contact with the whole tooth surface and away from much of the gum, giving even lightening over days of wear. Wikipedia notes that some colour change is lost over time.
